3. In due course, the auction was held and one Moheruddin Chowdhury, among others, participated in the bid and his bid was accepted by RAJUK. Accordingly, he paid 10% earnest money on the spot and subsequently paid a further 15% of the bid money on 31-3-1970. He also paid two further instalments. Later on, the allotment letter No. DIT/EO/3937 dated 21-8-1970 was issued and the possession of the suit land was also duly handed over on 22-9-1970 in his favour by issuing a certificate of possession. It is further stated in the petition that the said Moheruddin was in correspondence with the DIT for settlement of a dispute regarding the discrepancy in the rate of interest as stated in the auction notice and in the letter of allotment but subsequently, RAJUK by its Memo No. DIT/EO/1611/P dated 28-4-1980, referring to an earlier Memo dated 18-4-1977, informed Moheruddin Chowdhury that the allotment of the concerned plots stood cancelled. The RAJUK thereafter as it appears invited a fresh tender on 25-7-1981 for auction sale of the self-same plot Nos. 20 and 20A. As such, Moheruddin Chowdhury filed a writ petition being Writ Petition No. 597 of 1981, before, the High Court Division, challenging the legality of the memo dated 28-4-1980 contained in the Memo dated 22-7-1981, issued by the RAJUK but on promulgation of Martial Law in 1982, the said writ petition abated. Thereafter, the aforesaid Moheruddin Chowdhury, filed a suit being Title Suit No. 347 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dhaka against RAJUK, praying for a decree, amongst others, that the Memo No. DIT/EO/152-P dated 28-4-1980, canceling the allotment was illegal. The Rajuk contested the suit by filing written statement on 3-5-1983. In due course, the suit was decreed ex parte on 27-7-1991. In the meantime, Moheruddin Chowdhury the original allottee died and his heirs the petitioner Nos. 1 to 6 herein, filed an application before RAJUK for mutation of their names instead of their father, namely, late Moheruddin Chowdhury. Thereafter, RAJUK filed a Miscellaneous Case being Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree. After a contested hearing, the said ex parte decree was set aside by an order dated 30-8-1999 and the suit was restored to its file and number. Thereafter, the petitioners firstly filed an appeal being First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 236 of 1999. After hearing, the Hon'ble High Court Division by his Judgment and Order dated 15-11-2000 set aside the order dated 30-8-1999 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997 and allowed the appeal and upheld the aforesaid ex parte decree. But on an appeal before the Appellate Division being the Civil Appeal No. 231 of 2002, it transpired that the First Miscellaneous Appeal was wrongly filed before the High Court Division instead of a Civil Revision, as such, the Appellate Division sent the case back on remand to the High Court Division to convert the case into a civil revisional application. Accordingly, the said Miscellaneous Appeal No. 236 of 1999 was converted into Civil Revision No. 2221 of 2005. After hearing of the said converted civil revision, the High Court Division by its Judgment and Order dated 6-12-2005, set aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Third Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997, setting aside the earlier ex parte judgment and decree dated 27-7-1991 passed in Title Suit No. 347 of 1982 (Annexure E). 

 16. Their only case is that since it was leased out earlier in 1964, they are unable to comply with the direction of the High Court Division. When it was pointed out to them that the decree dated 24-7-1991 in Title Suit 347 of 1982 is binding on RAJUK, they promptly replied that the said Anwar Alam also filed a suit being Title Suit No. 113 of 2006, in the Court of Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka. 

 19. Mr TH Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the contemner opposite parties submits that since the petitioner obtained a decree in a civil suit the petitioner ought to have filed an execution case instead of coming to the contempt jurisdiction of this Court under Article 108 of the Constitution but no where in his affidavit in opposition or else where he raises such a contention. Obviously this is an off-the-cuff remark. 

 23. After a lapse of sometime the petitioners approached the RAJUK for mutation of their names then, as it appears, the RAJUK rose from its long slumber and filed a miscellaneous case being Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying for setting aside the ex parte decree. The said miscellaneous case was allowed by the judgment and order dated 30-8-1999 and the suit was restored. But on revision being Civil Revision No. 2221 of 2005, High Court Division rejected the miscellaneous case and affirmed ex parte decree and also directed execution and registration of the plots in favour of the petitioner by RAJUK. On appeal the Appellate Division affirmed the Judgment and Order of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision. The petition for review was also dismissed by the Appellate Division. 

 39. Challenging the said decree, the RAJUK filed a miscellaneous case being Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997, under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, on 24-11-1997 but nowhere in its petition it mentioned anything about allotment of the selfsame plots to Md Alauddin. 

 51. A State being the most law abiding Institution is bound by any declaration given by a Court of law. As such, no execution case is even necessary. Similarly, the various institutions of the State, be it is the Government or any statutory corporation is bound by the declaration and is expected to carry out such a declaration without any further direction in this respect since non-compliance of any decree, even if it is only by way of declaration, shows that the relevant institution is not law abiding. If any institution of the State chooses to defy law, there may be failure of the Rule of law, a basic structure of the Constitution. 

 52. In this case, the failure on the part of the officials of RAJUK to honour the decree is no doubt reprehensible but in the absence of specific direction, does not constitute contempt of Court. 

 53. The civil revision was in respect of the Order dated 30-8-1999; passed in the Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1997, setting aside the ex parte decree. As such, the question before the Court under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code; was not the decree itself but as to whether the defendant was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. The Subordinate Judge found that there was, and restored the suit but the High Court Division found otherwise, and set aside the Order passed in the miscellaneous case. But since the decree itself was not before the High court Division, its modification by giving a mandatory order was apparently without jurisdiction. 

 56. Although on a technical reason, the Rule is going to be discharged against the contemners but the entire saga of this case discloses a very unhealthy situation in RAJUK. However, this is for the Government to look into it. 

 57. This case itself raises these unanswered questions.
